sections.title: F. Join the two sentences with the word in brackets. Write ONE sentence (although / even though) or TWO sentences (however / nevertheless).

items.q: The job is well paid. I don’t like it. (although)
a: Although the job is well paid, I don't like it
I don't like the job although it is well paid
I don't like it although the job is well paid
Although the job is well-paid, I don't like it

items.q: It was raining. We went for a walk. (even though)
a: We went for a walk even though it was raining
Even though it was raining, we went for a walk

items.q: He works long hours. He’s always happy. (nevertheless)
a: He works long hours. Nevertheless, he's always happy
He works long hours. Nevertheless he's always happy

items.q: The hotel was expensive. It wasn’t very nice. (however)
a: The hotel was expensive. However, it wasn't very nice
The hotel was expensive. However it wasn't very nice

items.q: She’s very young. She’s an excellent manager. (although)
a: Although she's very young, she's an excellent manager
She's an excellent manager although she's very young

items.q: I studied a lot. I failed the exam. (even though)
a: I failed the exam even though I studied a lot
Even though I studied a lot, I failed the exam

items.q: The bus is slow. It’s cheap. (however)
a: The bus is slow. However, it's cheap
The bus is slow. However it's cheap

items.q: He didn’t get the job. He tried again next year. (nevertheless)
a: He didn't get the job. Nevertheless, he tried again next year
He didn't get the job. Nevertheless he tried again next year

sections.title: Listening. Listen to a careers adviser talking to students. Are the sentences true or false?
sections.script:
Hello everyone. Today I want to give you some advice about your first job interview. First, don't think only about money. Research shows that people who enjoy their work are often happier than people with very high salaries.
Second, prepare. Read about the company before the interview, and think of two or three questions you can ask them. Interviewers love students who are curious.
Third, you don't always need a university degree. For many jobs, companies are more interested in your skills — for example, if you can work well in a team or speak foreign languages.
And finally, don't be afraid of failure. My first three interviews went badly. But I learned something every time, and the fourth one was successful. So if you don't get a job, it isn't the end of the world — it's practice!

items.q: The adviser says money is the most important thing in a job.
She says you should prepare some questions for the interviewer.
She says you always need a university degree.
She thinks languages can be a useful skill.
Her first job interview was successful.

sections.title: G. Read the text. Match paragraphs A–E with questions 1–7. There are two extra questions.
sections.passage:
A  When Malika was eight, she watched a documentary about elephants and decided she wanted to be a vet. Her family laughed — nobody in her village had ever been to university.

B  At school she worked harder than anyone. Although her parents couldn’t pay for extra lessons, she studied biology from old books at the library every evening.

C  She failed her university exam the first time. ‘I cried for a week,’ she remembers. ‘Then I made a new plan.’ She worked in a pet shop for a year and studied at night.

D  The second time, she passed with one of the highest scores in the country. Five years later she qualified as a vet and opened a small clinic in her village.

E  Today Malika visits schools to talk to girls about science. ‘If you have a dream,’ she tells them, ‘don’t let anybody laugh at it.’

items.q: In which paragraph … does Malika give advice to young people?
… do we learn how her dream started?
… do we learn what she did after failing?
… do we learn how she studied without money for lessons?
… do we learn where she works now?
… do we learn how much she earns?
… does she describe her favourite animal?
